sessions.title: Introduction to the Online Typing Platform

sections.title: Big idea
sections.text: Speed and precision come from muscle memory built on your own typing style, and the platform tracks it for you.

sections.title: Key points
sections.text:
The platform logs your WPM, accuracy, and struggle keys.

Your baseline test is your starting point; every later score is compared to it.

Home row (ASDF / JKL;) is a useful anchor. Use a consistent, comfortable technique and return to your anchor after reaching for other keys. Keep wrists neutral and take short breaks. Practise letters, numbers, symbols and opposite-hand Shift as well as words.

Muscle-memory clusters: practise the key groups and sequences you personally miss most.

Speed and precision improve together through repeated, targeted drills.

sections.title: Check yourself
sections.text:
What are my top struggle keys on the platform?

Is my accuracy rising on those keys week to week?

sections.title: Big idea
sections.text: Word's ribbon is organised by purpose, so once you know where a tool lives you never have to guess.

sections.title: Key points
sections.text:
Home = fonts and paragraphs; Layout = margins; Insert = tables and headers.

Default margins are 1 in; a left-bound document uses a wider left margin.

Spacing: single = 1.0, double = 2.0.

First-line indent = 0.5 in.

sections.title: How to
sections.text:
1. Margins: Layout > Margins > Custom Margins > OK.

2. Spacing: Home > Line and Paragraph Spacing.

3. Indent: Home > Paragraph dialog launcher > Special > First line > 0.5 in.

4. Check your work with Show/Hide (the paragraph mark icon).

sections.title: Check yourself
sections.text:
Can I open page setup without help?

Which tab controls margins and which controls spacing?

sections.title: Big idea
sections.text: Proofreader's marks are a shared code between editor and typist; they only work if both know the meaning.

sections.title: Key points
sections.text:
Stet = leave as it was (dots under the text).

Caret (^) = insert.

Strike-through = delete.

Three lines under a letter = capitalise.

Transpose mark = swap letters or words.

New paragraph mark = start a new paragraph.

sections.title: How to
sections.text:
1. Scan the whole page before typing.

2. Apply each mark exactly as shown.

3. Proofread your typing against the marked copy.

sections.title: Worked example: marked copy and typed result
sections.text:
MARKED:  Thank you for you letter of 3 October.   (insert ^ r after 'you')

         the course starts on monday.            (capitalise the initial 't' and 'm')

         Please [delete: kindly] confirm.         (strike-through 'kindly')

TYPED:   Thank you for your letter of 3 October. The course starts on Monday. Please confirm.

sections.title: Check yourself
sections.text:
Can I name all six core marks without the chart?

Did I apply every correction on my last transcription?

sections.title: Big idea
sections.text: Letter style signals formality, and tab stops (not the spacebar) keep layout stable.

sections.title: Key points
sections.text:
Fully Blocked: every line at the left margin; fastest style.

Modified block: position the date and closing block at the specified tab stop, often near the horizontal centre. Paragraphs may remain blocked; indent the first line 0.5 in only when the requested style calls for it.

Open punctuation: no commas after the salutation or close.

Mixed punctuation: punctuation after the salutation and complimentary close, following the supplied style guide. Open, mixed and closed punctuation are not interchangeable. Follow the question or model rather than assuming one convention for all letters.

Yours faithfully goes with Dear Sir or Madam; Yours sincerely goes with a named person.

AMS simplified style is also named in the syllabus: use a subject heading and omit the salutation and complimentary close. Practise it with the supplied model. Letter layout is determined by the requested style, not simply by how formal the message feels.

sections.title: How to
sections.text:
1. Ruler: click at the position, then press Tab once.

2. Dialog: Home > Paragraph launcher > Tabs > position > Left > Set > OK.

3. Remove: drag the stop off the ruler, or Clear in the dialog.

sections.title: Worked example: Fully Blocked, Open Punctuation
sections.text:
Nassau Business Institute

Collins Avenue, P.O. Box N-9012

Nassau, The Bahamas

 

16 October 2026

 

Ms Andrea Knowles

Bahamas Freight Services

Nassau, The Bahamas

 

Dear Ms Knowles

 

Training courses for office staff

 

Thank you for your letter of 3 October. ...

 

Yours sincerely

 

 

T. Moss

Course Coordinator

sections.title: Check yourself
sections.text:
Which style suits a formal complaint? A quick update?

Does my date still line up after I change the font?

sections.title: Big idea
sections.text: Subject lines, enclosures, and cc notations tell the reader what is included and who else has the letter.

sections.title: Key points
sections.text:
Subject line: one blank line below the salutation; capitals, bold, or underline.

Enclosure notation: one blank line below the signature block.

cc lists others who receive a copy.

A continuation header (name, page number, date) goes on page 2 onward so separated pages can be reassembled.

sections.title: How to
sections.text:
1. Insert > Header > Edit Header > tick Different First Page.

2. Type the continuation details on page 2 only, then close the header.

sections.title: Worked example: ending a letter with special notations
sections.text:
Yours faithfully

 

 

J. Rolle

Sales Manager

 

Enc. Price list (2 pages)

cc: Finance Office

 

(Page 2 header: Island Office Supplies | Page 2 | 12 October 2026)

sections.title: Check yourself
sections.text:
If the pages were shuffled, could someone reorder them?

Does the header appear on page 2 only?

sections.title: Big idea
sections.text: Envelope layout follows how postal scanners read the envelope.

sections.title: Key points
sections.text:
Recipient address sits right of centre, single-spaced, 3 to 5 lines.

Return address is top left, about 0.5 in from the edges, 9 to 10 pt.

DL = 110 x 220 mm; C5 = 162 x 229 mm.

Special notations (such as CONFIDENTIAL) are typed separately from the address.

sections.title: How to
sections.text:
1. Mailings > Envelopes; Word may detect the delivery address from your letter; always verify it.

2. Edit the return address.

3. Choose Add to Document or Print.

sections.title: Worked example: envelope layout
sections.text:
Island Office Supplies Ltd.

Bay Street, P.O. Box N-1234

Nassau, The Bahamas

 

                          The Principal

                          Harbour View High School

                          Nassau, The Bahamas

sections.title: Check yourself
sections.text:
Does the envelope match the letter's inside address?

Is my return address small and top left?

sections.title: Big idea
sections.text: Memos skip the formal letter structure because sender and reader share the workplace.

sections.title: Key points
sections.text:
Header block: TO, FROM, DATE, SUBJECT.

No salutation or complimentary close; initials replace the signature.

Body is single-spaced, block format, one blank line between paragraphs.

Tab stops align the header entries.

sections.title: How to
sections.text:
1. Set one tab stop.

2. Type each label, press Tab once, then type the entry.

sections.title: Worked example: memo
sections.text:
MEMORANDUM

 

TO:       All Teaching Staff

FROM:     Vice Principal

DATE:      19 October 2026

SUBJECT:  Updated office hours

 

Office hours will change from 1 November. ...

 

(initials) JM

sections.title: Check yourself
sections.text:
Are all four header fields present and aligned?

Did I use Tab instead of the spacebar?

sections.title: Big idea
sections.text: Choose a table style according to how much structure the data needs.

sections.title: Key points
sections.text:
Boxed: full gridlines for dense comparison data.

Ruled: top, header, and bottom lines for financial summaries.

Open: no gridlines; tab alignment.

Centre the table the way you would centre a title.

sections.title: How to
sections.text:
1. Insert > Table.

2. Table Design > Borders.

3. Table Properties > Alignment > Center.

4. Use Distribute Columns Evenly to tidy widths.

sections.title: Check yourself
sections.text:
Does my table style fit how dense my data is?

Is any numeric text wrapping?

sections.title: Big idea
sections.text: Numbers are decimal-aligned so place values stack and can be compared at a glance.

sections.title: Key points
sections.text:
Text columns: left-align.

Whole numbers: right-align.

Decimals and currency: decimal-align.

Dollar sign on the first row and the total row only.

Total row: single line above, double line below.

sections.title: How to
sections.text:
1. Home > Paragraph dialog > Tabs.

2. Enter the position, choose Decimal, then Set and OK.

sections.title: Worked example: decimal-aligned ledger
sections.text:
Item                          Amount
Printer paper                 $12.50
Ink cartridges                 45.00
USB drives                      8.75
Total                         $66.25

These are line amounts, not unit prices. Use a single rule above the total and a double rule below it when the task specifies this accounting style.

sections.title: Check yourself
sections.text:
Do all my decimal points line up?

Is the dollar sign only where it should be?

sections.title: Big idea
sections.text: Size, boldness, and spacing control what the reader sees first; this is function, not decoration.

sections.title: Key points
sections.text:
Title 18 to 24 pt bold; subheadings 14 to 16 pt; body 11 to 12 pt.

Use at most two font families.

Borders and boxes isolate must-not-miss details.

Dot leaders link items to prices on menus.

sections.title: How to
sections.text:
1. Design > Page Borders.

2. Tabs dialog: right tab with a dotted leader.

3. Insert > Text Box for callouts.

sections.title: Worked example: menu with dot leaders
Check yourself
sections.text:
Where does my eye land first on my flyer?

Is that the most important detail?

sections.title: Big idea
sections.text: Deciding between a table and a display document is a skill: is the content data to compare, or a message to promote?

sections.title: Key points
sections.text:
Table = rows and columns to compare.

Display document = persuasion or event promotion.

Reuse decimal alignment and visual hierarchy rules.

sections.title: Check yourself
sections.text: Before typing, did I decide table or display, and why?

sections.title: Big idea
sections.text: A left-bound report needs a wider left margin because the binding takes space.

sections.title: Key points
sections.text:
Left margin 1.5 in; other margins 1 in.

Heading hierarchy: Main Title, Primary Heading, Paragraph Heading.

Double spacing leaves room for edits.

sections.title: How to
sections.text:
1. Layout > Margins > Custom Margins.

2. Set the left margin to 1.5 in.

sections.title: Check yourself
sections.text:
Would any text disappear into the binding?

Do heading sizes step down logically?

sections.title: Big idea
sections.text: Footnotes give evidence without breaking the flow of your argument.

sections.title: Key points
sections.text:
Footnote number is a superscript at the exact point of the claim.

Footnote text sits at the bottom of the same page below a divider.

Title page: title, author, date.

sections.title: How to
sections.text:
1. Click after the cited word.

2. References > Insert Footnote.

sections.title: Worked example: footnote
sections.text:
Typing instruction improves with drills.¹

 

_______

¹ Smith, J. (2020). Typing Skills. Nassau Press, p. 14.

sections.title: Check yourself
sections.text:
Is the footnote mark right at the claim?

Are footnotes numbered in sequence?

sections.title: Big idea
sections.text: Minutes record what was decided and who is responsible.

sections.title: Key points
sections.text:
Standard sections: Call to Order, Confirmation of Previous Minutes, Matters Arising, New Business, Adjournment.

An ACTION BY column names who is responsible.

Agenda items are numbered in order.

sections.title: How to
sections.text: 1. Insert > Table for the action-item list.

sections.title: Worked example: minutes skeleton
sections.text:
MINUTES OF STAFF MEETING, 19 October 2026

Present: ...   Apologies: ...

1.0 Call to Order

2.0 Confirmation of Previous Minutes

3.0 Matters Arising

4.0 New Business            ACTION BY: V. Rolle

5.0 Adjournment

sections.title: Check yourself
sections.text:
Could someone prove what was decided from these minutes?

Does every decision have an owner?

sections.title: Big idea
sections.text: Itineraries and forms are built to be scanned quickly, so clarity beats density.

sections.title: Key points
sections.text:
Group the itinerary by day.

Times or flights on the left, activities or hotels on the right.

Forms use boxed fields and shaded labels.

sections.title: How to
sections.text:
1. Click the cell.

2. Table Design > Shading > choose a light fill.

sections.title: Worked example: itinerary layout
sections.text:
DAY 1 - Monday 2 November

07:30   Flight BA-210 Nassau to Miami

12:00   Check in, Harbour Hotel

15:00   Meeting with suppliers

sections.title: Check yourself
sections.text:
Could I use this itinerary while rushing?

Are the form labels clearly shaded?

sections.title: Big idea
sections.text: Fix structural changes first and small edits second, or you will undo your own corrections.

sections.title: Key points
sections.text:
Pre-scan the whole page for 15 to 30 seconds.

Do moves and inserts first, then spelling and capitals.

Stet = leave it; strike-through = delete.

sections.title: Check yourself
sections.text:
Did I scan the page before typing?

Did I resolve every structural instruction?

sections.title: Big idea
sections.text: Naming the category of an error is what lets you fix it.

sections.title: Key points
sections.text:
Weak-finger substitution: the wrong finger hits a nearby key.

Transposition: letters swapped (the becomes teh).

Shift timing: the capital lands on the wrong letter.

Visual lag: eyes read ahead of the fingers.

sections.title: How to
sections.text:
1. Log each error with a category.

2. Drill that category.

sections.title: Check yourself
sections.text:
What is my number one error category?

Did my drill target it?

sections.title: Big idea
sections.text: Clean and steady usually beats fast and messy. For this classroom exercise, use the supplied five-word error penalty; official scoring must follow the actual paper and mark scheme.

sections.title: Key points
sections.text:
NWPM = (Gross Words - (Errors x 5)) / Time in Minutes.

Example: 250 gross words in 5 minutes with 3 errors gives (250 - 15) / 5 = 47 NWPM.

1-minute bursts build peak speed.

5-minute runs rebuild control.

Avoid sprinting at the start.

This is the formula in the supplied classroom notes, not a verified official BGCSE formula or the Dojo’s WPM calculation. Use the assigned definition of gross words; do not substitute a displayed WPM rate for a word count.

sections.title: Check yourself
sections.text: Did NWPM rise because I was faster or cleaner?

sections.title: Big idea
sections.text: Exams mix document types without labels, so recognise the type fast.

sections.title: Key points
sections.text:
TO / FROM header = memo.

Inside address and salutation = letter.

Rows and columns = table.

Recall the rules and tool steps from Sessions 4 to 15.

sections.title: Check yourself
sections.text: Did I identify the type before formatting?

sections.title: Big idea
sections.text: Knowing your own NWPM baseline lets you set a realistic exam target.

sections.title: Key points
sections.text:
Recap the NWPM formula.

Error penalties are heavy; clean beats fast.

Compare results to your Session 18 baseline.

This session is a speed-and-accuracy rehearsal, not a complete Paper 1. The supplied syllabus describes Paper 1 as five tasks across the content. Use a complete authorised paper and its stated timing for a full simulation.

sections.title: Check yourself
sections.text: What NWPM am I realistically aiming for?

sections.title: Big idea
sections.text: Budget exam minutes by document complexity, not evenly.

sections.title: Key points
sections.text:
Recap letter styles, punctuation, and envelope steps.

Plan your time before you start.

sections.title: Exam tips
sections.text:
Spend the first minute reading the whole paper and planning your order.

Do your strongest document first for early confidence.

Proofread carefully. Apply the actual paper’s mark scheme; the five-word classroom drill penalty is not a universal document-production rule.

sections.title: Check yourself
sections.text: How many minutes did the letter take, and was that right?

sections.title: Big idea
sections.text: Some formatting errors cost more marks than others; check those first.

sections.title: Key points
sections.text:
Decimal alignment and total-row formatting are high-value checks.

Keep two minutes at the end for checking.

sections.title: Exam tips
sections.text:
Spend more minutes on the letter than on the envelope.

Use the Mailings tool for the envelope to save time.

Check the inside address matches the envelope.

sections.title: Check yourself
sections.text: Did I check the highest-value items first?

sections.title: Big idea
sections.text: The mock is the diagnostic: apply everything under full exam conditions.

sections.title: Key points
sections.text:
No new content.

Note which section felt weakest.

A full paper, or both papers together, needs a separate extended sitting. Do not compress full official timing into a 90-minute lesson. Confirm the current paper instructions with your teacher.

sections.title: Exam tips
sections.text:
Check decimal alignment and total lines first.

Verify centred title and consistent font sizes.

Leave two minutes for a final read-through.

sections.title: Check yourself
sections.text: Which section felt weakest under pressure?

sections.title: Big idea
sections.text: Mock exam mistakes are fixable through targeted practice.

sections.title: Key points
sections.text:
Build a personal plan from your actual lost marks.

Reuse the error categories from Session 17.

sections.title: Exam tips
sections.text:
Review your scored mock with feedback, then retry the weakest section independently. Follow the actual rules during a separate full simulation.

Mark your own paper afterwards and write down every lost mark.

sections.title: Check yourself
sections.text: What single pattern must I fix before the final?

sections.title: Big idea
sections.text: Pacing, checking order, and tool steps should now be automatic.

sections.title: Key points
sections.text:
State your pacing plan aloud before you start.

Compare your final result with your Session 1 baseline.

A full paper, or both papers together, needs a separate extended sitting. Do not compress full official timing into a 90-minute lesson. Confirm the current paper instructions with your teacher.

sections.title: Exam tips
sections.text:
Sort lost marks into categories: layout, accuracy, time, or misreading instructions.

Practise your weakest category twice before the final.

Redo the weakest section and compare scores.

sections.title: Check yourself
sections.text: How far have I come since my baseline?

teacherLessons.title: Ergonomics, Home Row & Why Touch-Typing Works
teacherLessons.text:
Month 1 — Week 1   |   Duration: 75 minutes (post-Dojo)

Understanding Objective (not just a skill target):

Understand *why* eyes-off-keyboard typing is faster and more accurate long-term than hunt-and-peck, not just that it is 'correct.'

1. Diagnose & Question (10 min)

Time two volunteers typing the same short sentence — one hunting and pecking, one using a hint of touch-typing (even if slow). Ask the class: which one will get faster with practice, and why?

2. Direct Instruction — The Rule That Solves It (10 min)

Home Row Anchoring: Left hand A-S-D-F, Right hand J-K-L-; (F and J tactile bumps let fingers find home without looking).

Muscle memory principle: consistent finger-to-key mapping turns typing into an automatic reflex, freeing the brain to focus on content instead of key location.

Ergonomics: monitor at eye level 18-24 inches away, wrists neutral, feet flat — framed as prevention against strain from years of typing, not just a checklist.

3. Guided Production (35 min)

Students complete blind home-row drills (fff jjj fjf) with keyboard covers, then type simple home-row-only words (fall, flask, glad). Emphasize rhythm over speed.

4. Error Review & Reflection Checkpoint (10 min)

Peer posture check using a checklist; 2-minute home-row passage, target 15 WPM at 95% accuracy. Discuss: did looking at the keyboard cost you time or accuracy?

Materials Needed:

Keyboard covers/skins, typing software (TypingClub/Keybr), posture checklist handout.

teacherLessons.title: Full Keyboard Reaches, Shift Key & the Numeric Pad
teacherLessons.text:
Month 1 — Week 2   |   Duration: 75 minutes (post-Dojo)

Understanding Objective (not just a skill target):

Understand shift-key logic (opposite-hand pinky) as a system for never breaking home-row anchoring, and see the numeric keypad as its own small home-row system.

1. Diagnose & Question (10 min)

Show a sentence typed with Caps Lock left on by mistake, and a paragraph with numbers typed using the top-row number keys versus the numeric keypad. Ask: what's inefficient here?

2. Direct Instruction — The Rule That Solves It (10 min)

Top row (QWERTYUIOP) and bottom row (ZXCVBNM) reach patterns — fingers travel out and immediately return home.

Shift key rule: opposite-hand pinky presses Shift so the typing hand stays free to strike the letter.

Numeric keypad home position: index-4, middle-5 (tactile bump), ring-6 — same anchor-and-return logic as the main keyboard.

3. Guided Production (35 min)

Drills on vertical reach combinations, then a short paragraph mixing capitalized proper nouns and numeric data typed on the keypad.

4. Error Review & Reflection Checkpoint (10 min)

3-minute full-keyboard timed test, target 20 WPM/95% accuracy. Shift-key spot-check: are pinkies doing the work?

Materials Needed:

Full keyboards with numeric keypad, timed drill software, numeric worksheet.

teacherLessons.title: Word Interface Orientation & Page Setup
teacherLessons.text:
Month 1 — Week 3   |   Duration: 75 minutes (post-Dojo)

Understanding Objective (not just a skill target):

Understand the Word interface as a toolbox organized by purpose, and know the exact menu path for every formatting change introduced today — so production never requires guessing where a tool lives.

1. Diagnose & Question (10 min)

Hand students a page with visibly wrong margins (text crammed edge-to-edge), inconsistent spacing, and no paragraph indents. Ask: if you had to fix this, where would you even start looking in Word? Let them explore/guess before instruction.

2. Direct Instruction — The Rule That Solves It (10 min)

Ribbon orientation: tabs group related actions (Home = fonts/paragraphs, Layout = margins/orientation, Insert = tables/headers).

Margins exist to prevent text from being cut off in printing/binding — Default 1 inch; use the task’s binding allowance. The report lesson in this guide uses 1.5 inches on the left.

Line spacing (1.0 single, 2.0 double) and first-line paragraph indents (0.5 inch) both exist to make dense text easier to read and scan.

3. Teacher-Led Tool Walkthrough — Exact Click-Path (10 min)

Teacher demonstrates each step live on the projector; students follow along on their own screens before being released to work independently. No student begins production until every step below has been demonstrated and repeated once by the class together.

Setting margins: Layout tab > Margins button (in the Page Setup group) > choose a preset, or click Custom Margins at the bottom to open the Page Setup dialog box and type exact inch values > OK.

Setting line spacing: Home tab > Paragraph group > click the Line and Paragraph Spacing icon (the icon with horizontal lines and up/down arrows) > select 1.0 or 2.0 from the dropdown.

Setting a first-line paragraph indent: Home tab > click the small diagonal arrow in the bottom-right corner of the Paragraph group (the dialog box launcher) > this opens the Paragraph dialog > under Indentation, set 'Special' to 'First line' and enter 0.5 inch > OK.

Checking your work: turn on Show/Hide formatting marks (Home tab > paragraph symbol icon, ¶) to see exactly where returns, spaces, and indents actually landed.

4. Guided Production (25 min)

Students open Word, follow the same three steps just demonstrated to reformat the flawed page from the diagnose step: correct margins, correct line spacing, and correct first-line indents — then compare before/after readability.

5. Error Review & Reflection Checkpoint (10 min)

Practical check: given a new unformatted file, apply correct page setup, spacing, and indents in 15 minutes without teacher prompting. Discuss which fix mattered most for readability.

Materials Needed:

Computers with MS Word, sample unformatted text files, projector for live demonstration and before/after comparison.

teacherLessons.title: Proofreader's Marks as a Shared Editing Language
teacherLessons.text:
Month 1 — Week 4   |   Duration: 75 minutes (post-Dojo)

Understanding Objective (not just a skill target):

Understand proofreader's marks as a communication system between editor and typist — a shorthand that only works if both sides agree on its meaning.

1. Diagnose & Question (10 min)

Show a handwritten manuscript page marked up with proofreader symbols but no key/legend. Ask: could you type this correctly right now? What's missing?

2. Direct Instruction — The Rule That Solves It (10 min)

Core marks: Stet (leave it), Transpose, Capitalize, Delete, Insert caret (^), New Paragraph — each solves a specific communication gap between editor and typist.

Insertion vs. deletion marks follow a directional logic (arrows point to the exact insertion point; strike-through means permanently gone).

3. Guided Production (35 min)

Flashcard matching drill on 15-20 marks, then transcribing a short marked-up letter, converting handwritten instructions into a clean typed document using the Word skills from Week 3.

4. Error Review & Reflection Checkpoint (10 min)

Symbol identification quiz (target 100% on core marks); timed transcription of a 300-word marked draft with zero uncorrected markup errors.

Materials Needed:

Proofreader's marks reference chart, marked-up practice manuscripts, red pens for peer marking.

teacherLessons.title: Business Letter Styles as Solutions to Formality Levels
teacherLessons.text:
Month 2 — Week 1   |   Duration: 75 minutes (post-Dojo)

Understanding Objective (not just a skill target):

Understand that letter styles (Fully Blocked, Blocked, Indented) and punctuation styles (Open/Closed) signal formality, and know how to actually position the date/close using tab stops rather than the spacebar.

1. Diagnose & Question (10 min)

Show three real-looking letters — one fully blocked, one indented, one a messy hybrid built with spacebar taps that misaligns when the font changes. Ask: which looks most official, and why did the spacebar version break?

2. Direct Instruction — The Rule That Solves It (10 min)

Fully Blocked: everything starts at the left margin — fastest to produce, most common in modern business.

Modified Block/Indented: date and closing shifted to center — a more traditional, formal look.

Open Punctuation (no comma after salutation/close) vs. Closed Punctuation (comma after 'Dear Sir,') — connects to formality and speed trade-off.

3. Teacher-Led Tool Walkthrough — Exact Click-Path (10 min)

Teacher demonstrates each step live on the projector; students follow along on their own screens before being released to work independently. No student begins production until every step below has been demonstrated and repeated once by the class together.

Setting a custom tab stop: click directly on the horizontal ruler at the desired position (e.g., the 3.25-inch mark) to place a left tab stop; or Home tab > Paragraph dialog launcher > Tabs button > enter an exact position > Set > OK for precision.

Using the tab stop: press the Tab key once to jump the cursor to that exact position — never use multiple spacebar presses, which shift when fonts change.

Removing a tab stop: drag it off the ruler, or select it in the Tabs dialog and click Clear.

4. Guided Production (25 min)

Students format one Fully Blocked letter with Open Punctuation (no tabs needed) and one Indented letter with Closed Punctuation, using a ruler tab stop to position the date and closing.

5. Error Review & Reflection Checkpoint (10 min)

Timed production: error-free 150-200 word Fully Blocked letter in 12 minutes. Discuss: which style would you choose for a formal complaint letter vs. a quick client update?

Materials Needed:

BGCSE correspondence style guide, sample raw letter content, Word with ruler enabled.

teacherLessons.title: Special Letter Features & Multi-Page Continuation
teacherLessons.text:
Month 2 — Week 2   |   Duration: 75 minutes (post-Dojo)

Understanding Objective (not just a skill target):

Understand subject lines, enclosures, and cc notations as reader navigation aids, and know how to insert a header that only appears on page 2 onward.

1. Diagnose & Question (10 min)

Show a 2-page letter with no continuation header and no subject line. Ask: if these pages got separated, what problem occurs?

2. Direct Instruction — The Rule That Solves It (10 min)

Subject line answers 'what is this about' before reading the body.

Enclosure notation answers 'should something else have come with this.'

cc/bcc answers 'who else knows about this.'

Continuation header (Name/Page/Date) exists specifically to solve the 'pages got separated' problem just diagnosed.

3. Teacher-Led Tool Walkthrough — Exact Click-Path (10 min)

Teacher demonstrates each step live on the projector; students follow along on their own screens before being released to work independently. No student begins production until every step below has been demonstrated and repeated once by the class together.

Inserting a page-2-only header: Insert tab > Header button > Edit Header > in the Header & Footer Design tab, check 'Different First Page' so page 1 stays blank while page 2+ shows the header.

Typing the continuation content directly into the header area (Recipient Name / Page Number / Date), then Close Header and Footer to return to the body.

4. Guided Production (25 min)

Students format a 2-page executive letter with a subject line, enclosure notation, cc list, and a page-2-only continuation header.

5. Error Review & Reflection Checkpoint (10 min)

Benchmark: complete 2-page letter with all special notations in 20 minutes; check that the continuation header appears only on page 2.

Materials Needed:

Multi-page draft prompts, continuation header checklist.

teacherLessons.title: Envelope Formatting & Postal Logic
teacherLessons.text:
Month 2 — Week 3   |   Duration: 75 minutes (post-Dojo)

Understanding Objective (not just a skill target):

Understand envelope layout as driven by how postal sorting actually reads an envelope, and know how to generate a matched envelope directly from a letter in Word.

1. Diagnose & Question (10 min)

Show an envelope with the return address in the center and recipient address in a corner. Ask: would this get delivered correctly?

2. Direct Instruction — The Rule That Solves It (10 min)

Recipient address sits right-of-center where scanners expect it; return address top-left, small font.

Special notations (CONFIDENTIAL, AIR MAIL) placed where they'll be seen first without interfering with scan zones.

DL vs. C5 sizing driven by what's being mailed.

3. Teacher-Led Tool Walkthrough — Exact Click-Path (10 min)

Teacher demonstrates each step live on the projector; students follow along on their own screens before being released to work independently. No student begins production until every step below has been demonstrated and repeated once by the class together.

Generating an envelope: Mailings tab > Envelopes button > this opens the Envelopes and Labels dialog.

Word auto-fills the Delivery Address box if it detects an address in your open letter; type or edit the Return Address box manually.

Click Add to Document to insert the envelope as a new page, or Print if printing directly onto envelope stock.

4. Guided Production (25 min)

Students use the Envelopes and Labels tool to produce a matching envelope for the letter built in Session 2.1, plus one with a CONFIDENTIAL notation typed manually above the address block.

5. Error Review & Reflection Checkpoint (10 min)

Precision check against a postal template overlay; speed drill producing 3 envelopes in under 8 minutes.

Materials Needed:

Envelope stock or templates, Word Envelopes/Labels tool.

teacherLessons.title: Interoffice Memos — Internal Communication Shorthand
teacherLessons.text:
Month 2 — Week 4   |   Duration: 75 minutes (post-Dojo)

Understanding Objective (not just a skill target):

Understand why memos skip formal letter structure, and reuse the tab-stop skill from Session 2.1 to align a memo header block precisely.

1. Diagnose & Question (10 min)

Place a formal letter and a memo side by side. Ask: what's missing from the memo, and why doesn't that matter here?

2. Direct Instruction — The Rule That Solves It (10 min)

TO/FROM/DATE/SUBJECT header block — the internal equivalent of an inside address and subject line combined.

No complimentary close/signature — replaced by handwritten initials next to the sender's name.

Tab stops align header fields precisely — the same ruler technique from Session 2.1, applied to a new layout.

3. Guided Production (35 min)

Students format a policy memo from a handwritten draft, aligning the header block with the tab-stop method already learned.

4. Error Review & Reflection Checkpoint (10 min)

Timed test: 200-word memo in 10 minutes, zero tab misalignments. Month 2 wrap check: one letter + one memo in a single 35-minute session.

Materials Needed:

Sample memo drafts, BGCSE memo marking guide.

teacherLessons.title: Table Structures as Data Organization Choices
teacherLessons.text:
Month 3 — Week 1   |   Duration: 75 minutes (post-Dojo)

Understanding Objective (not just a skill target):

Understand that Boxed, Ruled, and Open table styles are chosen based on how much visual structure the data needs, and know how to actually insert and style a table in Word.

1. Diagnose & Question (10 min)

Show the same data three ways: dense boxed grid, minimal ruled lines, and plain tabbed text. Ask: which is easiest to scan?

2. Direct Instruction — The Rule That Solves It (10 min)

Boxed tables suit dense, comparison-heavy data.

Ruled tables suit financial summaries — a top rule, header rule, and bottom total rule direct the eye to the total without clutter.

Centering a table on the page mirrors how centering a title focuses the eye.

3. Teacher-Led Tool Walkthrough — Exact Click-Path (10 min)

Teacher demonstrates each step live on the projector; students follow along on their own screens before being released to work independently. No student begins production until every step below has been demonstrated and repeated once by the class together.

Inserting a table: Insert tab > Table button > drag across the grid to choose rows/columns, or click Insert Table for an exact number.

Changing border style: click inside the table, then the Table Design tab appears > use Borders dropdown to select All Borders (boxed) or apply borders to only top/bottom rows (ruled).

Centering the table: click inside the table > Table Layout tab (or right-click > Table Properties) > Table tab > Alignment > Center.

Adjusting column width: hover over a column border until the cursor changes, then drag; or right-click > Distribute Columns Evenly for auto-fit.

4. Guided Production (25 min)

Students build one boxed schedule table and one ruled financial summary from the same raw dataset, choosing which style fits which purpose.

5. Error Review & Reflection Checkpoint (10 min)

Practical test: construct a formatted table from raw data in 15 minutes; check for zero text wrapping in numeric columns.

Materials Needed:

Word Table Design tools, raw tabular datasets.

teacherLessons.title: Column Alignment as a Number-Reading Aid
teacherLessons.text:
Month 3 — Week 2   |   Duration: 75 minutes (post-Dojo)

Understanding Objective (not just a skill target):

Understand why numbers are right/decimal-aligned while text is left-aligned, and know how to set a decimal tab stop for currency columns.

1. Diagnose & Question (10 min)

Show a column of prices left-aligned versus decimal-aligned. Ask: which column lets you tell at a glance which price is bigger?

2. Direct Instruction — The Rule That Solves It (10 min)

Left-align text (names, descriptions) because we read text left to right.

Right-align whole numbers and decimal-align currency so digits stack by place value.

Dollar sign appears only on the first row and the total row — repeating it every row clutters the column.

3. Teacher-Led Tool Walkthrough — Exact Click-Path (10 min)

Teacher demonstrates each step live on the projector; students follow along on their own screens before being released to work independently. No student begins production until every step below has been demonstrated and repeated once by the class together.

Setting a decimal tab: Home tab > Paragraph dialog launcher > Tabs button > enter a ruler position > under Alignment select Decimal > Set > OK. Word will now align every number in that column on its decimal point when you press Tab.

Applying a single or double underline to a total row: select the row > Home tab > Borders dropdown (next to the underline icon in the table area) > Top Border for the single line above the total, Bottom Double Border for below it.

4. Guided Production (25 min)

Students build a 5-column financial ledger table with a decimal tab for currency and a properly ruled total line.

5. Error Review & Reflection Checkpoint (10 min)

Benchmark: 4-column financial table in 15 minutes with 100% correct decimal alignment.

Materials Needed:

Accounting-style raw data sheets, decimal tab practice sets.

teacherLessons.title: Display Documents — Designing for a Reader's Eye Path
teacherLessons.text:
Month 3 — Week 3   |   Duration: 75 minutes (post-Dojo)

Understanding Objective (not just a skill target):

Understand visual hierarchy (size, bold, spacing) as controlling what a reader sees first, and know how to apply page borders and font-size hierarchy in Word.

1. Diagnose & Question (10 min)

Hand students a single dense, unformatted block of text advertising a school event. Ask: where does your eye go first? Where should it go first?

2. Direct Instruction — The Rule That Solves It (10 min)

Visual hierarchy: largest/boldest element = most important info, then key details, then fine print — max 2 font families to avoid competing signals.

Borders and callout boxes isolate must-not-miss details from the rest of the flow.

Dot leaders connect two related pieces of information across empty space.

3. Teacher-Led Tool Walkthrough — Exact Click-Path (10 min)

Teacher demonstrates each step live on the projector; students follow along on their own screens before being released to work independently. No student begins production until every step below has been demonstrated and repeated once by the class together.

Adding a page border: Design tab (or Layout tab in some versions) > Page Borders > choose a style/width in the Borders and Shading dialog > OK.

Adjusting font size for hierarchy: Home tab > Font Size box > type or select a larger number (e.g., 24pt for the title, 14pt for subheadings, 11pt for body).

Creating dot leaders: Home tab > Paragraph dialog launcher > Tabs button > enter a right-aligned tab position > under Leader select the dotted-line option (option 2) > Set > OK.

Adding a callout box: Insert tab > Shapes or Text Box > draw the box, then type inside it and apply a border/fill from the Shape Format tab.

4. Guided Production (25 min)

Students redesign the ugly announcement from the diagnose step into a flyer with clear hierarchy, then build a short menu using dot leaders.

5. Error Review & Reflection Checkpoint (10 min)

Design portfolio check: one flyer + one menu within 25 minutes each, evaluated on hierarchy and balance, not just correctness.

Materials Needed:

Ugly unformatted announcement sample, borders/shading tools in Word.

teacherLessons.title: Month 3 Consolidation & Mixed Practice
teacherLessons.text:
Month 3 — Week 4   |   Duration: 75 minutes (post-Dojo)

Understanding Objective (not just a skill target):

Understand tables and display documents as related tools for the same goal — making information easy to scan — by choosing the right one for a new scenario using only tools already taught.

1. Diagnose & Question (10 min)

Present three new raw content scenarios (a price list, a conference schedule, a comparison chart). Ask students to decide, before typing: table or display document, and why?

2. Direct Instruction — The Rule That Solves It (10 min)

Decision framework: use a table when data has consistent rows/columns to compare; use a display layout when the goal is persuasion or event promotion.

Recap decimal alignment and visual hierarchy rules from the previous two sessions as a checklist, not new content.

3. Guided Production (35 min)

Students complete two of the three scenarios independently, applying the decision framework and the exact tool steps already demonstrated.

4. Error Review & Reflection Checkpoint (10 min)

Month 3 assessment: one table + one display document under timed conditions, graded on whether the format choice fit the content.

Materials Needed:

Three new raw content scenarios, Month 3 rubric.

teacherLessons.title: Reports & Manuscripts — Margins That Serve a Physical Purpose
teacherLessons.text:
Month 4 — Week 1   |   Duration: 75 minutes (post-Dojo)

Understanding Objective (not just a skill target):

Understand the 1.5-inch left-bound margin as a physical necessity, reusing the Page Setup skill from Month 1 with a new value.

1. Diagnose & Question (10 min)

Show a mock-up of a report bound on the left with 1-inch margins — text visibly disappearing into the binding. Ask: what happened, and what would fix it?

2. Direct Instruction — The Rule That Solves It (10 min)

Left-bound margin allowance: 1.5 inch left vs. 1 inch on other sides — the extra 0.5 inch is the 'gutter' the binding consumes.

Heading hierarchy (Main Title > Primary Heading > Paragraph Heading) mirrors an outline — bigger/bolder means broader scope.

Double spacing in manuscripts exists so an editor has room to write corrections by hand between lines.

3. Guided Production (35 min)

Students format a left-bound report with correct margins (via Layout > Margins > Custom Margins, as learned in Month 1) and a full heading hierarchy using font sizes from Month 3.

4. Error Review & Reflection Checkpoint (10 min)

Margin audit: verify exact 1.5-inch left margin; check heading sizes decrease logically down the hierarchy.

Materials Needed:

BGCSE report style guide, raw report text, ruler for margin verification.

teacherLessons.title: Footnotes, Citations & Title Pages
teacherLessons.text:
Month 4 — Week 2   |   Duration: 75 minutes (post-Dojo)

Understanding Objective (not just a skill target):

Understand footnotes as a way to give evidence without breaking the flow of the main argument, and know how to insert one automatically rather than typing it manually.

1. Diagnose & Question (10 min)

Show a paragraph with a claim and no source, next to the same paragraph with a footnote. Ask: which is more trustworthy?

2. Direct Instruction — The Rule That Solves It (10 min)

Footnote numbers appear as superscript at the exact point of the claim; footnote text sits below a divider line at the bottom of that same page.

Title pages front-load identifying information so a reader knows what they're holding before reading a word of content.

3. Teacher-Led Tool Walkthrough — Exact Click-Path (10 min)

Teacher demonstrates each step live on the projector; students follow along on their own screens before being released to work independently. No student begins production until every step below has been demonstrated and repeated once by the class together.

Inserting a footnote: place the cursor after the word needing a citation > References tab > Insert Footnote button. Word automatically adds the superscript number and drops the cursor to the bottom of the page for you to type the note.

Word handles the divider line and page-bottom placement automatically — you only need to type the citation text.

4. Guided Production (25 min)

Students add a title page and two footnoted citations to the report started in the previous session, using Insert Footnote rather than manual formatting.

5. Error Review & Reflection Checkpoint (10 min)

Citation audit: correct footnote numbering sequence and divider line placement, zero missing title page elements.

Materials Needed:

Sample footnoted reports, title page templates.

teacherLessons.title: Meeting Documentation — Agendas & Minutes as Organizational Memory
teacherLessons.text:
Month 4 — Week 3   |   Duration: 75 minutes (post-Dojo)

Understanding Objective (not just a skill target):

Understand minutes as a legal/organizational record where every structural element exists so an absent person can reconstruct what happened, using table and heading tools already taught.

1. Diagnose & Question (10 min)

Show a set of messy handwritten meeting notes with no structure. Ask: could someone prove what was decided and who's responsible for it, from these notes alone?

2. Direct Instruction — The Rule That Solves It (10 min)

Standard minutes sections (Call to Order, Confirmation of Previous Minutes, New Business, Adjournment) create a reconstructable timeline.

'ACTION BY' column/tag exists specifically to answer 'who is responsible.'

Agenda numbering (1.0, 2.0, 3.0) previews the meeting's structure before it happens.

3. Guided Production (35 min)

Students format a complete Minutes document from handwritten notes, including an action-item column built as a simple table (Insert > Table, from Month 3).

4. Error Review & Reflection Checkpoint (10 min)

Structural integrity check: verify every standard section is present and every decision has a named action owner.

Materials Needed:

Handwritten meeting note samples, Agenda/Minutes templates.

teacherLessons.title: Travel Itineraries & Admin Forms
teacherLessons.text:
Month 4 — Week 4   |   Duration: 75 minutes (post-Dojo)

Understanding Objective (not just a skill target):

Understand itinerary and form layouts as designed for someone scanning under time pressure, reusing table and shading tools already taught.

1. Diagnose & Question (10 min)

Show a disorganized paragraph describing a 3-day trip versus a structured day-by-day itinerary table. Ask: which one could you actually use while running through an airport?

2. Direct Instruction — The Rule That Solves It (10 min)

Itinerary structure groups by day, then time/flight on the left, activity/hotel on the right.

Admin forms (invoices, expense claims) use boxed fields and shaded labels so a person filling it in never has to guess where information goes.

3. Teacher-Led Tool Walkthrough — Exact Click-Path (10 min)

Teacher demonstrates each step live on the projector; students follow along on their own screens before being released to work independently. No student begins production until every step below has been demonstrated and repeated once by the class together.

Shading a table cell/label: click inside the cell > Table Design tab > Shading dropdown > choose a light fill color to distinguish label cells from fillable blank cells.

4. Guided Production (25 min)

Students format a 3-day itinerary and a simple expense claim form using table-based boxed structures with shaded label cells.

5. Error Review & Reflection Checkpoint (10 min)

Month 4 comprehensive check: one report excerpt + one itinerary within 40 minutes.

Materials Needed:

Sample flight/hotel data, invoice and expense claim templates.

teacherLessons.title: Decoding Complex Handwritten Manuscripts
teacherLessons.text:
Month 5 — Week 1   |   Duration: 75 minutes (post-Dojo)

Understanding Objective (not just a skill target):

Understand manuscript correction as prioritized problem-solving: structural changes must be resolved before micro-edits, or later fixes get undone.

1. Diagnose & Question (10 min)

Give students a manuscript with both a paragraph-move instruction and several small spelling corrections. Ask: if you fix the spelling first and then move the paragraph, what could go wrong?

2. Direct Instruction — The Rule That Solves It (10 min)

Pre-scan strategy: read the whole marked page once (15-30 seconds) before typing anything.

Priority order: structural moves and inserts first, then micro-edits.

Stet vs. strike-through: distinguishing 'leave it' from 'permanently delete.'

3. Guided Production (35 min)

Students transcribe a complex 300-400 word handwritten draft with layered corrections, applying the pre-scan-then-prioritize method and all Word tools taught to date.

4. Error Review & Reflection Checkpoint (10 min)

Manuscript exam: 15-minute transcription, no more than 2 uncorrected errors, 100% compliance with structural instructions.

Materials Needed:

BGCSE past-paper handwritten drafts.

teacherLessons.title: Error Diagnostics — Understanding Your Own Mistakes
teacherLessons.text:
Month 5 — Week 2   |   Duration: 75 minutes (post-Dojo)

Understanding Objective (not just a skill target):

Understand that errors have categories (weak finger, transposition, shift-timing, reading-ahead lag) — diagnosing the category is what actually fixes the error.

1. Diagnose & Question (10 min)

Give students their own error log from earlier sessions. Ask: do you see a pattern — same letters, same finger, same position in a word?

2. Direct Instruction — The Rule That Solves It (10 min)

Common error categories: weak-finger substitution, transposition, shift-timing, and visual lag.

Targeted remediation drills exist for each category.

3. Guided Production (35 min)

Students review their personal error logs, identify their top error category, and complete a targeted drill matched to that category.

4. Error Review & Reflection Checkpoint (10 min)

Self-diagnosis accuracy check: can the student correctly name their own dominant error pattern and explain why the targeted drill addresses it?

Materials Needed:

Individual error logs from prior sessions, category-specific drill sets.

teacherLessons.title: Speed Building Without Sacrificing Accuracy
teacherLessons.text:
Month 5 — Week 3   |   Duration: 75 minutes (post-Dojo)

Understanding Objective (not just a skill target):

Understand the speed/accuracy trade-off as a real curve, and learn the NWPM formula as a way to measure it instead of guessing.

1. Diagnose & Question (10 min)

Have two students race the same passage — one sprints and makes errors, one goes steady and clean. Calculate NWPM for both live. Ask: who actually 'won'?

2. Direct Instruction — The Rule That Solves It (10 min)

Net Words Per Minute (NWPM) = (Gross Words - (Errors x 5)) / Time in Minutes.

Burst drills (1-minute) build peak speed; longer drills (5-minute) rebuild control.

Pacing: avoiding an initial sprint preserves accuracy stamina.

3. Guided Production (35 min)

Students complete a 1-minute burst drill followed by a 5-minute paced drill, calculating their own NWPM after each.

4. Error Review & Reflection Checkpoint (10 min)

Milestone check: minimum 40 NWPM with no more than 3 errors on a 5-minute test.

Materials Needed:

Timed software with live WPM/accuracy tracking, NWPM calculation worksheet.

teacherLessons.title: Month 5 Mixed Document Marathon
teacherLessons.text:
Month 5 — Week 4   |   Duration: 75 minutes (post-Dojo)

Understanding Objective (not just a skill target):

Understand that real exam conditions mix document types unpredictably — the goal is applying the right mental model and toolset quickly.

1. Diagnose & Question (10 min)

Present three short raw prompts back-to-back (a letter excerpt, a small table, a memo) with no labels. Ask: how do you quickly recognize which document type this is?

2. Direct Instruction — The Rule That Solves It (10 min)

Recognition cues: header fields signal memo; inside address + salutation signals letter; row/column structure signals table.

Recap of Month 2-4 core rules and tool steps as a rapid-fire checklist.

3. Guided Production (35 min)

Students complete all three mixed prompts under light time pressure, self-identifying document type before applying formatting.

4. Error Review & Reflection Checkpoint (10 min)

Marathon check: three documents completed correctly within 45 minutes total, each correctly identified before formatting began.

Materials Needed:

Mixed unlabeled raw prompts, Month 2-4 rule checklists.

teacherLessons.title: Paper 1 Speed & Accuracy Simulation
teacherLessons.text:
Month 6 — Week 1   |   Duration: 75 minutes (post-Dojo)

Understanding Objective (not just a skill target):

Understand exam-day pacing strategy — knowing your own NWPM baseline lets you set a realistic target.

1. Diagnose & Question (10 min)

Review each student's best NWPM from Month 5. Ask: what target should you set for the real exam?

2. Direct Instruction — The Rule That Solves It (10 min)

A timed-copy classroom rehearsal, not a complete official Paper 1: the supplied syllabus describes five tasks across the content.

Review of NWPM scoring and error-penalty awareness under real pressure.

3. Guided Production (35 min)

Full timed copy test under strict exam conditions, no assistance.

4. Error Review & Reflection Checkpoint (10 min)

Compare the classroom timed-copy result with the personal Month 5 baseline. Score any complete official paper with its own mark scheme.

Materials Needed:

Official BGCSE past Paper 1 copy texts, timer.

teacherLessons.title: Paper 2 Simulation — Correspondence & Envelopes
teacherLessons.text:
Month 6 — Week 2   |   Duration: 75 minutes (post-Dojo)

Understanding Objective (not just a skill target):

Understand exam time-budgeting across multiple documents using tools already mastered.

1. Diagnose & Question (10 min)

Show last year's Paper 2 correspondence section. Ask: how many minutes can you realistically spend on the letter versus the envelope?

2. Direct Instruction — The Rule That Solves It (10 min)

Time-budgeting strategy: allocate minutes per document based on complexity, not evenly.

Recap letter styles, punctuation, and envelope tool steps as an exam-speed checklist.

3. Guided Production (35 min)

Full past-paper correspondence section completed under timed exam conditions.

4. Error Review & Reflection Checkpoint (10 min)

Score against official mark scheme; debrief on time allocation accuracy.

Materials Needed:

BGCSE past Paper 2 correspondence sections, official mark scheme.

teacherLessons.title: Paper 2 Simulation — Tables & Display Documents
teacherLessons.text:
Month 6 — Week 3   |   Duration: 75 minutes (post-Dojo)

Understanding Objective (not just a skill target):

Understand which formatting decisions are worth double-checking under time pressure versus which can be done quickly.

1. Diagnose & Question (10 min)

Ask students: which single formatting error costs the most exam marks if missed? Where should your final 2-minute check focus?

2. Direct Instruction — The Rule That Solves It (10 min)

Prioritized checking strategy: decimal alignment and total-row formatting flagged as highest-value checks.

Recap table typologies and display hierarchy tool steps.

3. Guided Production (35 min)

Full past-paper table and display document section under timed conditions.

4. Error Review & Reflection Checkpoint (10 min)

Score against mark scheme; debrief on where marks were lost.

Materials Needed:

BGCSE past Paper 2 table/display sections, mark scheme.

teacherLessons.title: Full Mock Exam — Paper 1 & 2 Combined
teacherLessons.text:
Month 6 — Week 4   |   Duration: 75 minutes (post-Dojo)

Understanding Objective (not just a skill target):

Understand the complete exam experience end-to-end, applying pacing and prioritization strategies learned across the previous three sessions.

1. Diagnose & Question (10 min)

No diagnose step — this session is the diagnostic. Students take the full mock and generate their own data for the review session.

2. Direct Instruction — The Rule That Solves It (10 min)

N/A — full simulation session.

3. Guided Production (35 min)

Schedule a separate extended sitting for the selected paper(s), using the actual paper instructions for timing and breaks. This cannot fit into the regular 35-minute production block.

4. Error Review & Reflection Checkpoint (10 min)

Full scoring against official mark schemes for both papers.

Materials Needed:

Complete past-paper set (Paper 1 + Paper 2), exam-hall conditions (silence, strict timing).

teacherLessons.title: Review & Targeted Remediation
teacherLessons.text:
Month 6 — Week 5   |   Duration: 75 minutes (post-Dojo)

Understanding Objective (not just a skill target):

Understand personal weak points from the mock exam as fixable through targeted practice, not as fixed limitations.

1. Diagnose & Question (10 min)

Return scored mock exams. Ask each student: what pattern do you see in your lost marks?

2. Direct Instruction — The Rule That Solves It (10 min)

Individualized remediation plans built from actual mock-exam error patterns.

Recap of any document type or tool step where the class collectively struggled.

3. Guided Production (35 min)

Students complete targeted practice matched to their own error pattern from the mock.

4. Error Review & Reflection Checkpoint (10 min)

Improvement check: repeat the weakest section of the mock exam and compare scores.

Materials Needed:

Scored mock exams, category-specific remediation drills.

teacherLessons.title: Final Exam Simulation
teacherLessons.text:
Month 6 — Week 6   |   Duration: 75 minutes (post-Dojo)

Understanding Objective (not just a skill target):

Confirm readiness by replicating full exam conditions one final time, with strategy and tools fully internalized.

1. Diagnose & Question (10 min)

Ask students to state their own pacing plan out loud before starting.

2. Direct Instruction — The Rule That Solves It (10 min)

Final recap of pacing, prioritized checking, and error-penalty awareness — no new content, only reinforcement.

3. Guided Production (35 min)

Schedule a separate extended sitting for the final paper set under its stated exam conditions; do not compress it into the regular lesson production block.

4. Error Review & Reflection Checkpoint (10 min)

Final scoring against official mark scheme; compare full trajectory from Month 1 baseline to final result.

Materials Needed:

Final BGCSE past-paper set, exam-hall conditions.
